prompt: What did deleting one order from `lake/flat` do to the Parquet file that held it?
hint: Parquet files are never edited.

choices.text: Edited the row out of the file, in place
choices.why: A Parquet file cannot be edited in place; Delta never changes a file it has written.

choices.text: Nothing: a new file got the other rows, and a commit stopped naming the old one
choices.why: Right. The old file is still on disk; it is simply no longer in the table.

choices.text: Deleted it from the disk and wrote a smaller one in its place, under the same name
choices.why: Only vacuum deletes files from disk, and it had not run.

choices.text: Appended a tombstone row to the end of it
choices.why: Nothing is appended to a written Parquet file.

prompt: `lake/flat` held 98,727 orders in one file. How many rows did deleting one order have to copy?
hint: Every row of the file but the deleted one.

prompt: After the delete, a colleague counts the orders with DuckDB over `lake/flat/*.parquet` and gets 197,453. Why?
hint: What does a glob over the folder ignore?

choices.text: The delete failed halfway and wrote the whole month a second time into the folder
choices.why: The delete worked: the log's version 1 has 98,726 rows.

choices.text: DuckDB counts deleted rows until vacuum runs
choices.why: DuckDB knows nothing of deletes here; it read files.

choices.text: It read the folder: the old file and the new
choices.why: Right. Only a reader of the log knows the old file is out of the table.

choices.text: The zstd file stores each row twice
choices.why: The codec changes the size, not the rows.

prompt: Two jobs finish writing their Parquet files at the same moment and both try to commit version 8 of the same table. What stops both from succeeding?
hint: A commit is one file with a number for a name.

choices.text: The commit file is created only if no file of that name exists; the loser retries as version 9
choices.why: Right. The store's "create only if absent" is the whole lock, which is why no lock service was needed.

choices.text: A lock service beside the storage account, which Delta needs on Azure
choices.why: `deltalake` wrote to Azurite in lesson 17 with no lock service.

choices.text: Nothing; both commit and the table has two version 8s
choices.why: Two files cannot have the same name, and the second creation fails.

choices.text: Delta allows one writer per table, so the second job was never started
choices.why: Writers do not ask permission to start; they find out at the commit.

prompt: In a commit, the ___ action takes a file out of the table and leaves it on disk.
hint: Its opposite is `add`.

prompt: In `lake/by_day`, where is the `dt` of each order kept?
hint: Look at the schema the Parquet file printed.

choices.text: In a `dt` column inside every Parquet file
choices.why: The partitioned files have no `dt` column; their schema lists six columns.

choices.text: In the folder's name and in the log
choices.why: Right. The reader puts the column back from there, and filters on it without opening a file.

choices.text: In the Parquet footer's statistics only
choices.why: The footer describes the columns inside the file, and `dt` is not one of them.

choices.text: In a separate partition index file that the library keeps beside the log
choices.why: There is no such file; the log and the folders are all there is.

prompt: The month question read 2,442,170 bytes from `by_day`, which holds 1,879,174 bytes on disk. How can a reader read more than there is?
hint: Each daily file is about 60 KB.

choices.text: The partition values were read once per row
choices.why: Partition values come from the log, not from the files.

choices.text: DuckDB read every file twice to check them
choices.why: Nothing checks files by reading them twice.

choices.text: The first read, for the footer, fetched each small file whole, and the columns were read again
choices.why: Right. A file smaller than that first read is read whole and then partly again.

choices.text: The log's JSON was counted as data
choices.why: `measure.py` counted only what crossed the tap, which the dataset opened: the Parquet files.

prompt: `lake/daily` has no partition column, yet the question about one day opened 1 file of 31. How did the reader know which?
hint: Each file was written by one night's append.

choices.text: It opened each footer and stopped at the right one
choices.why: It opened one file, not 31 footers.

choices.text: Each file's statistics in the log say its smallest and largest `dt` are that day
choices.why: Right. That is data skipping, and it needs no folders, only files written in the order they are asked about.

choices.text: The file names carry the date
choices.why: The names are random; the date is not in them.

choices.text: `deltalake` quietly partitions every table by its date column, whether asked to or not
choices.why: `daily` was written with no `partition_by`, and has no `dt=` folders.

prompt: Deleting the same order copied 98,726 rows in `lake/flat` and 2,998 in `lake/by_day`. How many times fewer rows did the partitioned table copy, to the nearest whole number?
hint: Divide one by the other.

prompt: Support often looks up one customer's orders, so somebody proposes partitioning the orders table by `customer_id`. What happens to the dashboard's question about one day?
hint: How many folders hold one day's orders?

choices.text: It gets faster, since each folder is smaller
choices.why: Smaller folders help only a question that names a customer.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the day is still in the log
choices.why: Each customer's file holds many days, so its `dt` range rules little out.

choices.text: It opens thousands of tiny files, one per customer
choices.why: Right. Every customer may have ordered that day, so every folder is opened, and each file costs more to open than it holds.

choices.text: It fails, since a partitioned table can be filtered only on its partition column
choices.why: Any column can be filtered; the partition decides only what can be skipped.

prompt: Which of these let a reader skip a file without opening it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Whatever the reader learns before it opens anything.

choices.text: The partition value recorded for the file
choices.why: Yes: it is in the path and the log.

choices.text: The smallest and largest values in the file's `add` statistics
choices.why: Yes: that is data skipping.

choices.text: The row-group statistics in the Parquet footer
choices.why: They let a reader skip parts of a file, after opening it to read the footer.

choices.text: The commit's `commitInfo`
choices.why: It records who did what and when, nothing about values.

prompt: What did compacting `lake/hourly` change?
hint: Count the rows before and after.

choices.text: The rows, which were sorted and deduplicated
choices.why: Compaction changes no row; its actions say `dataChange=false`.

choices.text: The files: 527 small ones became 31
choices.why: Right. Same 98,727 rows, one file per day.

choices.text: The partitions, which went from days to months
choices.why: The partitions stayed `dt`; each day was compacted within itself.

choices.text: Nothing in the table, only the disk, where the small files were deleted
choices.why: It is the other way round: the table changed and the disk kept the old files.

prompt: After compaction the disk held 558 Parquet files for a table of 31. Why?
hint: Compaction is a commit like any other.

choices.text: The 527 small files left the table and stayed on disk until vacuum
choices.why: Right. 527 old plus 31 new is 558.

choices.text: Compaction failed halfway and left both
choices.why: It committed: version 527 names 31 files.

choices.text: The checkpoints are Parquet files too
choices.why: The count left out `_delta_log`, where the checkpoints are.

choices.text: Each new file was written once per partition column and once per sort column
choices.why: Each day became one file, written once.

prompt: Every action of the compaction commit says `dataChange=false`. Who is that for?
hint: Think of a reader that wants only what is new.

choices.text: Vacuum, which keeps files marked that way forever, whatever the retention
choices.why: Vacuum removes what no recent version names, whatever the flag.

choices.text: A job that reads only what is new
choices.why: Right. It skips the commit instead of reading the month again as 31 new files.

choices.text: DuckDB, which refuses files with that flag
choices.why: DuckDB read the compacted table normally.

choices.text: The person reading the history, and no program
choices.why: Programs read it: a reader that follows changes depends on it.

prompt: Quitanda's loader appends to the orders table every hour from 7 to 23. When should the partition `dt=2026-10-15` be compacted?
hint: Compacting a partition that is still being written is wasted work.

choices.text: After every hourly load, to keep it at one file all day
choices.why: Seventeen rewrites of a growing day, where one would do.

choices.text: Once a month, together with every other day
choices.why: A month of dashboards reads the small files first.

choices.text: Once, after the day's last load
choices.why: Right. The day is then closed, and one rewrite leaves it at one file for good.

choices.text: Never; vacuum merges small files on its own
choices.why: Vacuum deletes files; it merges nothing.

prompt: What does vacuum delete?
hint: It is the one operation that deletes data files.

choices.text: Rows that a delete has marked
choices.why: A delete already rewrote the files; vacuum works on whole files.

choices.text: Commits older than seven days from `_delta_log`
choices.why: The log has its own retention; vacuum deletes data files.

choices.text: Data files that no version within the retention period names
choices.why: Right. Files the current version names are kept, whatever their age.

choices.text: The current version's small files, which compaction replaces
choices.why: Vacuum never touches a file the current version names.

prompt: After `vacuum 0 force`, `table.py lake/hourly@100 files` still prints 101 files and 18,577 rows, and `read` fails. Why the difference?
hint: What does each one open?

choices.text: `files` reads only the log, which still describes version 100; its data files are gone
choices.why: Right. The log outlived the files.

choices.text: `files` uses a cache that vacuum does not clear
choices.why: Each run opens the table afresh; there is no cache between runs.

choices.text: Vacuum deleted the log of version 100 but not its files
choices.why: It is the other way round.

choices.text: `read` failed because the table is locked while vacuum runs
choices.why: Vacuum had finished; the error names a missing file.

prompt: `deltalake` refused a vacuum with zero hours of retention because its default retention is ___ hours, seven days.
hint: Seven times twenty-four.

prompt: A customer asks to be erased, and their orders are deleted from the table on a Monday. Retention is seven days and vacuum runs on Sundays. When are the rows gone from the disk?
hint: A file becomes eligible seven days after the delete, and something has to remove it.

choices.text: On Monday, the moment the delete commits
choices.why: The delete takes the rows out of the table; the old files stay on disk.

choices.text: The following Sunday, six days later
choices.why: On that Sunday the old files are six days old, inside the seven-day retention, so vacuum keeps them.

choices.text: The second Sunday, 13 days later
choices.why: Right. The first vacuum past the seven days is the second Sunday; until then the rows can be read by travelling back.

choices.text: Never, as long as time travel is switched on for the table
choices.why: Time travel is not a switch; it lasts as long as the files do.

prompt: `by_day` read 73,813 bytes for the day question. At a thousand times the size, asked 4,464 times a month, at an illustrative 5 USD per terabyte processed (a terabyte being 10^12 bytes), what is the month's bill in USD, to two decimals?
hint: Bytes × 1,000 × 4,464, then divide by 10^12 and multiply by 5.

prompt: Why does the lesson count the cost of small files in files opened, rather than multiplying their bytes by a thousand like the rest?
hint: What sets how many files there are?

choices.text: Small files are free to read by the byte
choices.why: Bytes are billed the same whatever the file.

choices.text: Their number is set by how many writes there are, not by how much the table holds
choices.why: Right. At a thousand times the orders, an hourly load still writes 17 files a day, only bigger.

choices.text: Requests cost more than bytes at every size
choices.why: Which costs more depends on the sizes; that is what the tables compare.

choices.text: Compaction makes the bytes of small files irrelevant
choices.why: Before compaction the bytes are read; the lesson measured them.

prompt: Match each operation on a Delta table to what it writes.
hint: Only one of them deletes anything from disk.

pairs.right: New files with the other rows, and a commit that removes the old ones
Fewer, larger files, in a commit marked as no change to the data
Nothing new: it deletes old files from disk and records two commits
A commit whose files are those of an older version

right_distractors: An edit inside an existing Parquet file

prompt: Put the steps of a delete on a Delta table in the order they happen.
hint: Readers must never see half of it.
items: The new Parquet file, with every other row, is written where no reader looks
The next numbered commit is created, removing the old file and adding the new
A reader that starts now reads the new version
Vacuum, past the retention, deletes the old file from disk
